lawyer:
K.S. Nabi, A. F. Ali Asgar ----- For the Petitioner. 
S. R. Paul, with S. M. Haque ----- For the Respondent
parties:
A. Z. Rafiqul Ahmed  ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Laboratories, Mirpur Road, Dhanmondi, Dacca and ors  ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This rule under Article 102 of the Constitution calls in question an order dated 22-8-77 (Annexure-G) of respondent No. 3, Director, Bangladesh Council of Scientific & Industrial Research Laboratories, hereinafter referred to as the Council' dismissing the petitioner from service on ground of misconduct. 

 2. Case of the petitioner is that he joined the service of the Council in 1962 as a Junior Technician and by dint of merit and efficient discharge of duties he was promoted 10 the post of Technician on 10.9.65. He was again promoted as Senior Technical on 10.9.68. He was served with a notice dated 12.10.76 in which it was alleged that he had entered the office of the Superintendent, Establishment Branch on 24.6.76 and misbehaved with him. He submitted an explanation denying the allegation and nothing more was heard about it thereafter. But he was again charge sheeted en 4.5.77 on the same allegation of misbehavior with the Superintendent and was asked to show because why certain minor punishment would not be imposed on him. He submitted an explanation denying the allegation But he was suddenly served with an order dated 22.8.77 in which it was stated that he was dis-missed from his service en the said allegation contained in the charge-sheet dated 4.5.77, although he had been, charged with some minor offence punishable by censure, stoppage of increments etc. He submitted a representation to the respondents demanding justice. Thereupon, the respondents informed him that he was in fact dismissed in connection with a different proceeding drawn on a charge-sheet dated 15.3.77 and not in connection with the proceeding started on the charge-sheet dated 4.5.77. Since the respondents did not withdraw the order of dismissal he moved this octet and obtained the rule challenging the legality of the order of dismissal on the ground that it was in contravention of rules, vocative of constitutional provisions and malafide and seeking a declaration that it was made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 3. The respondents entered appearance and contested the application by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. They slated therein that two separate proceedings had been started against the petitioner. The proceeding started by charge-sheet dated 4.5.77 related to misbehavior of the Petitioner or with the Superintendent on 24.6.76, whereas the other proceeding started by a charge sheet dated 15.3.77 related to his 'misconduct' with the Derelict of the Council himself on 17.2.77. It has stated in the affidavit in opposition that the petitioner, on 17.2.77 at 9.30 a.m. accompanied by 30 Class III and Class IV employees of the Council trespassed into the office roam of Dr. Kamaluddin, Director of the Council, abused him in objectionable language and forced him to put his signature on a paper relating to house, subsidy of the employees. On that allegation the petitioner was first suspended from service and then a formal charge-sheet dated 15.3.77 to this effect was submitted to him. He was asked to show because why he would not be dismissed from service for his misconduct with the Director. On receipt of this charge-sheet the petitioner submitted his explanation on 23.3.77 admitting that he had entered the Director's Kern and Trussed for certain demands as to house subsidy but explained that he did not misbehave with the Director nor did he force him to put his signature on any paper. The respondents not being satisfied with his explanation, it was further stated, appointed a Committee of enquiry consisting or three senior officers of the Council to enquire into the matter. The Enquiry Committee after holding an enquiry submitted a report holding him guilty of gross misconduct. This report was accepted by the Council and the petitioner was dismissed by the impugned order of the Council. It was explained that while issuing the order of dismissal the date and number of the charge sheet were wrongly stated i.e. instead of the charge-sheet No. 1-24/76 Part/893 dated 15.2.77 the other charge-sheet namely, Sectl/Estt/1-24/ 76/1516 dated 4.5.77 was mentioned by a clerical mistake. 

 7. Mr. Ali Asgar, the learned Advocate has strenuously argued that though the Council was not established under any statute yet the Resolution of the Government creating the Council is, for all practical purposes, a law and that when the Council is performing functions of public character controlled by the Government on all important matters it takes the nature of a Statutory Corporation. A statutory corporation; he has argued, has now been included in the definition of 'a local authority'. A local authority as defined by the General Clauses (Amendment) Order, 1972, the President's Order No. 147 of 1972 is: "a Pourashava, Zilla Board, Union Panchayet, Board of Trustees of a port or other authority legally entitled .to, or entrusted by the Government with, the control or management of a municipal or local fund or any corporation or other body or authority constituted or established by the Government under any law." From the above definition it is clear that to constitute a local authority, a body or organisation must be established under any law or it must be legally entitled to or entrusted with the control or management of a municipal or local fund. In either case the establishment of the body or organisation shall have to be made under any law, or entrustment of any local fund shall be made "legally" that is to say, by or under any law. A Resolution of the Government, such as the one in question, issued from the Ministry of Natural Resources, Scientific & Technological Research is certainly not a law and as such the Council though engaged in the discharge of some functions having public character is not a local authority; it requires to be established by a law. A Resolution of the Government is not a law since it is not made or issued in exercise of any law-making power of the President. 

 8. Mr. K.S. Nabi, the learned Advocate applaud today and placed before us a recent Ordinance-Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Ordinance, 1978, Ordinance No. V of 1978 and on the strength of this Ordinance he has re-enforced the contention of Mr. Asgar that the Council is a local authority. This Ordinance has come into force on 2nd February, 1978 and it has been made and promulgated by the President in pursuance of the Proclamation of the 20th August, 1975 and 8th November, 1975 and in the exercise of all powers enabling him in that behalf. This Ordinance is of course, a law as referred to in the General Clauses (Amendment) Order, 1972. This Ordinance provides for the establishment of a Council to be called "The Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research" by a notification in the official gazette. Further it provides that the said Council when established shall be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal with power, subject to the provisions of this Ordinance, to acquire, hold and dispose of property and shall by the said name sue and be sued. It may be noted that these ingredients and authorities were absent in the case of the Council established under the Resolution dated 16.11.73. Section 29 of this Ordinance provides that on the establishment of the Council under this Ordinance, the previous Council established under the Resolution of the Government dated 16.11.73 shall stand dissolved an all assets, liabilities and properties of the Council and services of all officers, advisers and employees thereof shall stand transferred to the new Council. This section further provides that all suits and other legal proceedings instituted tic against tale former Council before its dissolution "shall be deemed to have been instituted by or against the Council" under this Ordinance. Mr. Nabi has contended that with the promulgation of this Ordinance, the Council established under the Resolution has become a statutory body falling within the definition of a local authority. The Council as referred to in the Ordinance Bangladesh, Council of Scientific and Indus trial Research Ordinance (V of 1978) may fall within the definition of a local authority, The Council as referred to in the ordinance may fall within the definition of a local authority but no Council will come into existence automatically on the promulgation of the Ordinance. The Council shall have to be established by the Government by a separate notification in the gazette. On the abasement of a Council under section 3 of the Ordinance, the Resolution dated 16.11.73 shall stand -"revoked" and the 'Council' established thereunder shall stand 'dissolved'. It is upon such dissolution that the assets, right, liabilities, officers, employees of the dissolved Council shall stand transferred to the newly established Council. In this case, there is no evidence whatever that the Government has established any Council peeler the Ordinance. 

 10. 'Even if we hold that the application was maintainable treating the Cc until as a body established by the Government under the Resolution dated 16.11.73 for performing some functions of public character, still Mr. Nabi will have an up-hill task to make out a case for our interference with the impugned order of-respondents. The terms and conditions of the petitioners service were not regulated by any statutory rules or .any regulations made by the Council with the Government's approval. Nevertheless, the Council applied the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 197.6 in the case of its employees and it also appears form the charge-sheet dated 15.2.77 Annexure 'G' that the petitioner proceeded against according to the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, briefly the Rules of 1976. The allegation brought against the petitioner constitutes "misconduct" calling for major punishments including dismissal from service under these Rules. Contention of the petitioner is that no 'enquiry was held into the allegation brought against him as required under these Rules and that he was not given reasonable opportunity to defend himself. But on perusal of the affidavit-in-opposition it is found that the petitioner was first given 7 days' time to show 'cause why he would not be dismissed from service on the allegation that he had committed misconduct with his Director by trespassing into his office accompanied by a large number of employees and forcing him to sign a paper indicating his accepting the employees' demand for house-subsidy. He submitted an explanation denying the allegation of "misconduct" but admitting that he had entered the Director's Office room without any permission. To enter the office-room of a superior officer without permission is by itself misconduct but in this case the petitioner had entered the office accompanied by a large number of other employees in order to press their demands. The respondents have stated that a Committee of Enquiry was constituted with three Senior Officers of the Council which held an enquiry and submitted a report finding the petitioner guilty of misconduct. When the alleged act was done in the presence of the Director, further enquiry except the Director's report and the delinquent's explanation was necessary for taking action against the petitioner in the interest of service discipline. The Contention that the petitioner was not given opportunity to defend himself or that no enquiry was held got no substance. 

 12. Mr. Nabi has contended that though the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules were not applicable to the petitioner but when the respondents themselves applied them in the case of their employees; those Rules should have been strictly followed in the pet toner's case also. From what has been discussed above it is clearly found that the respondents applied those Rules in the petitioner's case. 

 13. The last contention of Mr. Nabi is that the impugned order is malafide in that it was made without proper application of mind. He has argued that it was made in connection with a proceeding drawn by charge-sheet dated 4.5.77 which called for a minor punishment but the petitioner has been awarded a major punishment, dismissal. This action, Mr. Nabi contends is vocative of all canons of justice and fair play. Yes, if the petitioner had been charged with the commission of a minor offence but was punished for a major offence, the impugned order will be contrary to law as well as the principle of natural justice. But on perusal of the affidavit in opposition along with the clarification of the Respondents in Annexure-E we find that this contention got no basis whatever. It is on record that two proceedings were drawn against the misconduct. with the Director committed on 24.2.77 in which connection he was suspended, and the other was drawn on 4.5.77 on the allegation of misbehavior committed with the Superintendent on 24.6.76. The petitioner submitted his explanation in each of the two proceedings. The former called for a major penalty and the latter called for a minor penalty. Annexure-E clearly shows that the impugned order was passed in connection with the proceeding started by the charge-sheet dated 15.3.77 but in issuing the order, the number and dated of the other proceeding was stated by clerical mistake. This clarification is quite satisfactory and the mistake hardly affects the merit of the case. We also do not find any substance in the contention that the impugned order was made in haste or without proper application of mind. 

 14. We have discussed these questions touching the merit of the application in view of a recent decision of the Supreme Court in a case reported in 29 D.L.R. 41. Their Lordships have laid down a principle of great public importance in that case holding that employees of statutory corporations charged with duties of public character, even if their service conditions are not governed by statutory rules, cannot be treated as mere servants under the ordinary law of master and servant's but they are entitled to invoke the principles of natural justice in the case of wrongful dismissal from service. Further, it has been held that the principles of natural justice in such cases required a pre-hearing according to the principle "audi adteram partem". This broad principle of natural justice is found to have been followed in the petitioner's case. So we find that on merit also there is hardly anything to interfere with the impugned order. In the result, the rule is discharged, without, however, any order as to costs. The prayer for special leave to appeal is made but is refused.
